clue.text: Fund opportunity to see West Indies being dismissed by England

indicators.note: in cricket terms the West Indies side is sent off and England takes its place in the word

parts.note: a window is a chance or gap in which to see something
WI is the standard abbreviation for the West Indies cricket team

explanation.surface: A cricket report: the West Indies are bowled out by England, giving a fund a chance to see something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being dismissed by' swaps WI out of WINDOW and puts E in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: To fund something is to provide it with money, which is what an endowment does, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: High-flier — probably not putting much in — getting this result

definitions.meaning: a large bird of prey that soars at great heights

definitions.text: probably not putting much in — getting this result
definitions.meaning: in golf, a score two under par on a hole, usually meaning very few putts were needed

explanation.surface: A golfer who shoots high is praised, though their putting barely features in the result.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf an eagle is two strokes under par, so a golfer who gets one has likely needed only a putt or none at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird is a classic high-flier, and in golf the same name is given to a hole finished two under par.

clue.text: Tragedy perhaps engulfing Switzerland's former capital

indicators.note: one word swallows the other, so the second piece sits inside the first

parts.note: a tragedy is an example of drama
CH is the international code for Switzerland (Confoederatio Helvetica)

explanation.surface: A tragic story about Switzerland's old seat of government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' here means money, not a seat of government: the drachma was Greece's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital can mean money, and this was the Greek currency until the euro replaced it, hence former money.

clue.text: Unexpectedly, wage rises do double as 13 work with 18 for inspiration

indicators.note: the letters fall out in an unforeseen order, so they are rearranged
the word 'as' is to be used twice over

explanation.surface: A puzzling economics line: pay rises doubling, as a writer works from another novel for ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpectedly' rearranges WAGERISESDO with ASAS ('double' gives 'as' twice). Jean Rhys wrote this novel as a prequel to Jane Eyre, telling the story of Rochester's first wife.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1966 novel by Jean Rhys imagines the earlier life of Bertha Mason from Charlotte Brontë's book, so that book inspired it.

clue.text: Extend scope of attack to include US property

indicators.note: the first piece takes the second within it

parts.note: a bout is a spell or attack, as of illness
a ranch is a large farm estate in America

explanation.surface: A military plan widens its target to take in an American estate.
explanation.definitionFit: To branch out is an idiom for widening one's activities into new areas, so extending scope.

clue.text: Result of fighting to live without servant

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
a lackey is a servant or footman

explanation.surface: Fighting to survive without anyone to serve you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here: B and E wrap round LACKEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A bruised eye socket is a typical injury from a punch, so it results from fighting.

clue.text: Thoreau, regardless of fame, ultimately, may be construed as such

definitions.text: Thoreau, regardless of fame, ultimately, may be construed as such

indicators.note: to construe is to interpret, here to rework the letters into a new order
the letter is disregarded, so it is dropped from the name
points to the final letter of the word fame

explanation.surface: Henry David Thoreau, even without his reputation, can be called a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives E, the last of 'fame'; 'regardless of' drops it from THOREAU to leave THORAU, which 'may be construed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Thoreau wrote Walden, so the whole clue describes him as a writer, fame or no fame.

clue.text: Famous 5 in novel start to tease bachelor rotten

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters are made into something new
the opening letter of the word tease

explanation.surface: A famous figure in a novel teases a rotten bachelor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to' gives T from 'tease'; 'novel' rearranges it with BACHELOR and ROTTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: 5-down gives author, and the writer of Jane Eyre is one of the best known English authors.

clue.text: In Rigoletto, Verdi definitely went over the top

indicators.note: the letters lie within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: An opera critic says Verdi certainly overdid things in Rigoletto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals letters inside 'RigolettO VERDI Definitely', spanning three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdo something is to go too far with it, the same idea as going over the top.

clue.text: Monarch in the vanguard for that reason

indicators.note: the monarch's letters are set within the word 'the'

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
the fore is the front position, the vanguard

explanation.surface: A king leads from the front, and that is why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the vanguard' reads as one phrase, but 'the' stands alone and the monarch goes 'in' it; ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the usual crossword monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions introduce a consequence, so they are synonyms for 'hence'.

clue.text: Relative performance indicator for American students gains currency in Africa

indicators.note: the first piece acquires the second inside it

parts.note: GPA is grade point average, the US measure of a student's grades
the rand is South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: A financial report: an American grading index gains value in an African currency.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandfather is a family member, so a relative.

clue.text: Swingers' bar!

parts.note: looks like a nightclub for promiscuous couples but means the bar acrobats swing from

explanation.surface: A nightspot for wife-swapping couples.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a club for swingers; the real swingers are circus acrobats on a horizontal bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The suspended crossbar a circus aerialist swings on is literally a bar for swingers.

clue.text: Character displayed by those cycling

indicators.note: letters go round, with the end letter moved to the front

explanation.surface: Personality shown by people who ride bikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' takes the final E of THOSE round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the distinctive spirit or nature of a person or group, its moral character.

clue.text: Weeklong courses about distance learning

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the abbreviation
as a verb, courses means runs about, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for distance in physics formulae

explanation.surface: Week-long distance-learning courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'courses' rearranges WEEKLONG; 'about' puts that round D. 'distance learning' looks like one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning, as a noun, is what one has come to know, so knowledge and learning are synonyms.

clue.text: 5 rearranged 18 using extremes of speech, rather than central characters

indicators.note: the resulting letters are put into a new order
one set of letters replaces another

parts.note: 18-across is Jane Eyre
the two middle letters of the novel's title

indicators.note: the two outer letters of the word speech

explanation.surface: An author reworked another novel, using the edges of speech instead of the main characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes of' gives S and H from 'speech'; 'rather than' puts them where the two middle letters EE stood, giving JANSHYRE, and 'rearranged' sorts that.
explanation.definitionFit: 5-down is author, and Jean Rhys is the Dominica-born writer of novels such as Good Morning, Midnight.

clue.text: Judge does something about kinky book's coverage of soldiers' legs

indicators.note: the action's letters go round the rearranged book

parts.note: acts means takes action, does something

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of book are twisted

explanation.surface: A judge acts over a kinky book about soldiers' uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kinky' gives KBOO, which 'about' puts inside the word for does something; the definition is the closing phrase after the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackboots are tall military boots reaching the knee, so they cover soldiers' legs.

clue.text: Workplace reveals something, withholding papers under review

indicators.note: reviewing here means looking back over, so the letters are read backwards
the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: to out a secret is to reveal it
ID is identification papers

explanation.surface: An office exposes something while keeping documents under examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withholding' makes OIDUTS, which 'under review' then reads backwards; 'reveals something' is the verb to out, as in outing a secret.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's or broadcaster's studio is the room where they do their work.

clue.text: Story receiving record investment for right material

indicators.note: the story takes in the record's letters
the record is put in place of the letter for right

parts.note: a parable is a moral story
LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A tale of a record investment in the proper fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receiving' and 'investment for' together swap the R of PARABLE for LP. 'material' is an adjective here, not cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Material as an adjective means physical or tangible, and palpable means able to be touched.

clue.text: Smart accessory makes little difference to car tax

indicators.note: the letters are only slightly altered, one being shifted along

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: A smart add-on barely changes how much car tax you pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes little difference to' moves the A of CARVAT one place, after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A cravat is a neck scarf worn with smart dress, an elegant accessory.

clue.text: Church attendant upset some taking part in impropriety locally

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read backwards
only some letters of the phrase take part, lying inside it

explanation.surface: A church helper is upset by some local wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some taking part in' finds ETYLOCA inside 'impropriETY LOCAlly', and 'upset' turns it upward.
explanation.definitionFit: An acolyte assists the priest at services, carrying candles, so is a church attendant.

clue.text: 6 work one month with miserable beast, getting nothing out of him

parts.note: Jan is short for January

indicators.note: the letter for nothing is taken out of the gloomy donkey's name

parts.note: Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A miserable creature gains nothing from a month of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of him' takes O from EEYORE, the glum donkey of A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1847 novel is Charlotte Brontë's best-known book, so it is her work.

clue.text: Violent drawing of American head of state being decapitated

parts.note: a Yank is an American

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, is cut off

parts.note: a king is a head of state

explanation.surface: An American monarch is beheaded in a brutal image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being decapitated' cuts K from KING. 'drawing' means pulling, not a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing means pulling, and a yank is a sharp, forceful pull, so yanking is violent pulling.

clue.text: Said band made a harsh sound

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so it is replaced by one pronounced the same

parts.note: braid is a woven band used as trimming

explanation.surface: A music group is reported to have made a grating noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' suggests musicians, but it is a strip of braid.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's bray is a loud harsh cry, so to have brayed is to have made such a noise.

clue.text: Computer start-up in role reversal, pursuing high-street retailer

indicators.note: one piece follows behind the other

parts.note: Boots is a UK chain of chemists found on every high street

indicators.note: the word for role is turned back to front

parts.note: a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: A tech start-up takes on a role reversal, chasing a big shop chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversal' gives TRAP and 'pursuing' puts it after the chemist chain. 'start-up' means a computer booting, not a new firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootstrapping is the process of loading a computer's operating system as it starts up.

clue.text: Really up for it or really gutted?

parts.note: emptying this word leaves its first letter R and its last Y, said as a phrase

explanation.surface: A cheeky question: is someone keen for sex, or bitterly disappointed?
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' strips the inside of 'really', leaving R and Y: the phrase 'R and Y' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Randy is British slang for sexually eager, so up for it.

clue.text: Provide youth leader with discipline after losing head

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word youth
the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a field is a subject or discipline of study

explanation.surface: Give a youth leader some discipline once he has lost his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' gives Y; 'after losing head' cuts F from FIELD.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give or produce, as land yields crops, so it means provide.

clue.text: Every so often Monday is OK to make return journey

indicators.note: only every other letter is used
the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: yes and OK both signal agreement

explanation.surface: Monday is fine now and then for a trip home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every so often' takes ODYS from 'mOnDaY iS'; 'return' turns YES into SEY.
explanation.definitionFit: An odyssey is a long eventful journey, named after Odysseus's voyage home.

clue.text: Source of heat in contact with plastic fibre cladding

indicators.note: the rearranged letters cover the other piece
plastic means mouldable, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: on means touching, as a book on a table

explanation.surface: A heater touching plastic fibre insulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic' gives BFIRE, which 'cladding' wraps around the short word for touching; 'plastic' looks like a material beside fibre but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor fire of piled wood gives off heat, so it is a heat source.

clue.text: Turn after smashing up desk to run away

indicators.note: the first piece comes after the second
the desk is broken apart and its letters rebuilt

parts.note: to addle is to go bad, as milk turns sour

explanation.surface: Someone smashes up a desk, then turns and flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashing up' gives SKED, which 'after' places first. 'Turn' is to go off, as milk turns, which is what addle means.
explanation.definitionFit: Skedaddle is informal for leaving in a hurry, fleeing.

clue.text: Gradually move closer to land with border

parts.note: to edge is to move forward little by little

indicators.note: the closing letter, the last one, of the word land

parts.note: land given a border, i.e. bordered

explanation.surface: A boat creeps nearer to a shore that has a boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closer to land' looks like nearing the shore, but 'closer' is the last letter, D, of 'land'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something edged has a trim or rim along it, so it is bordered, as a lawn edged with flowers.
